summary: Jalisco combines high recorded lethality with legislative resistance. In the 2024 national state-by-state count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people it sits immediately behind the top two jurisdictions (the federal capital first with 17, including 11 trans women). Its congress then voted down extending gender recognition to minors in March 2025 in open defiance of a Supreme Court ruling obliging states to provide recognition procedures - placing Jalisco among the states actively refusing to implement the national standard for trans people's documents. Border-area reporting from the neighbouring state also documents rising attacks in municipalities on the Jalisco frontier, with gay-men killings attributed to named municipalities there.

sources.summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying Human Rights Watch news feature (31 March 2025) reviews progress and remaining challenges for trans rights in Mexico - state-level gender-recognition reform, pending legislation and violence/impunity - the country-level frame against which each state's deviation is scored.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024): documents how the absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure in Tabasco exposes trans people to police stops, denial of documents and institutional mistreatment - the country's clearest case of administrative erasure, cited to establish what a state without any procedure does to trans residents and visitors.

The Guardian global-development report (24 July 2024): Mexico City criminalised transfeminicide with sentences up to 70 years after the 2016 killing of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro whose attacker was released despite footage and witnesses and remains at large; activists call the law a watershed in one of Latin America's deadliest countries for trans people, while the reporting notes convictions lag the statute - the benchmark for judging other states' transfeminicide laws.
